skills.name: benchmarking

skills.name: build
skills.description: Guide for building, formatting, linting, and spell-checking Nanvix with z. Use this when asked to build or validate the repository.

skills.name: ci-cd-pipeline
skills.description: Guide for Nanvix CI and GitHub Actions workflow behavior, including local pipeline execution and matrix coverage. Use this when asked about CI checks, workflow failures, or release flow.

skills.name: coding-standards
skills.description: Detailed Nanvix coding, documentation, and review standards across Rust, C/C++, Python, and Shell. Use this when asked to implement or review code quality conventions.

skills.name: daemon-development
skills.description: Guide for developing and debugging Nanvix daemons, including guest daemons and host linuxd behavior. Use this when asked about daemon architecture or daemon changes.

skills.name: gdb-debugging
skills.description: Guide for debugging Nanvix guests using GDB remote debugging over the microvm machine type. Use this when asked about attaching GDB, setting breakpoints, or stepping through kernel code.

skills.name: kernel-development
skills.description: Guide for modifying and debugging the Nanvix kernel architecture and kernel-call paths. Use this when asked about kernel internals or kernel implementation changes.

skills.name: library-development
skills.description: Guide for creating and modifying Nanvix libraries under src/libs, including guest no_std and host std crates. Use this when asked about library architecture or crate changes.

skills.name: test
skills.description: Guide for running Nanvix tests with z. Use this when asked to run unit tests, integration tests, or the full test suite.

skills.name: test-development
skills.description: Guide for writing, running, and debugging Nanvix unit, integration, and system tests in Rust and C/C++. Use this when asked about test implementation or failures.

skills.name: troubleshooting
skills.description: Guide for diagnosing Nanvix build, runtime, and test failures, including cleanup and debugging workflows. Use this when asked to investigate errors or unstable behavior.

skills.name: user-app-development
skills.description: Guide for developing, building, and running Nanvix user-space applications across supported runtimes and languages. Use this when asked about guest app implementation or execution.

skills.name: pptx
skills.description: Use this skill any time a .pptx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates, layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.

skills.name: ast-consistency
skills.description: AST-level exec fidelity checking tools and pre-approved deviations. Use after modifying source files to verify exec code is unchanged.

skills.name: body-removal
skills.description: Remove function bodies from Rust/Verus source files to produce signature-only views. Used before the view-design phase to prevent implementation anchoring.

skills.name: bug-reporting
skills.description: Classify and report bugs found during Verus verification. Distinguishes true bugs from missing constraints and verifier limitations. Use when a verification failure might indicate a code bug.

skills.name: caller-analysis
skills.description: Analyze callers of a Rust module to understand usage expectations for Verus verification. Produces a caller-perspective analysis covering all functions with their visibility and call relationships.

skills.name: crate-analysis
skills.description: Principles for verification order in multi-file Rust crates. Verify leaf modules first so downstream modules can reference upstream specs directly. The pipeline tool handles ordering automatically.

skills.name: proof-extraction
skills.description: Extract large inline proof blocks from exec code into named lemmas in .proof.rs. Use when polishing verified code to improve readability and proof organization.

skills.name: proof-minimization
skills.description: Remove redundant proof artifacts (assertions, lemmas, hints, dead code) without weakening guarantees. Use when polishing verified code to reduce verbosity.

skills.name: property-analysis
skills.description: How to analyze source code and identify verification properties — the WHAT of verification. Covers module understanding, property discovery across four dimensions (functional correctness, safety, liveness, structural consistency), and quality review. Use this skill when deciding what to verify for a new module, writing property_analysis.md, or updating global_properties.md.

skills.name: proving-guide
skills.description: Proving methodology and mindset for Verus verification: function-by-function approach, persistence through failures, clean verification, and bug reporting. Use when writing proofs or resolving verification failures.

skills.name: review-methodology
skills.description: Review Verus verification code with focus on spec quality and automated checks.

skills.name: spec-completeness
skills.description: Detect specification incompleteness via nondeterminism checking. Given a Verus function spec, automatically determine whether the spec uniquely determines the output for each valid input. If not, use type-guided binary search to construct a concrete witness (input + two valid but different outputs). No LLM needed — pure SMT-based.

skills.name: spec-design
skills.description: How to write good Verus specs. Covers spec quality principles (anti-patterns, error paths), spec classification (internal, external-top, external-bottom trust boundaries), View abstraction design, and static vs dynamic enforcement. Use when writing or reviewing Verus specs.

skills.name: verus-constraints
skills.description: Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code.

skills.name: verus-setup
skills.description: Set up Verus formal verification infrastructure for a Rust project. Covers workspace-level config (vstd dependency, cfg flags, version pinning, Makefile, scripts) and per-crate config (metadata, cfg-gated includes, spec/proof stubs). Use this skill when preparing a repo or crate for Verus verification, adding make verify support, or integrating cheating detection into a build.

skills.name: verus-syntax
skills.description: Verus attribute-based syntax reference for exec functions. Covers #[verus_spec], #[verus_verify], proof!{}, proof_decl!{}, loop invariants. See GUIDE.md for advanced patterns, syntax_attr.rs for the official example.

skills.name: view-design
skills.description: How to design a View type that represents abstract state from the caller's perspective. Input: caller analysis + property concepts. Must NOT see implementation code.

skills.name: customize-cloud-agent
skills.description: Skill for customizing the Copilot cloud agent (formerly known as Copilot coding agent) environment, including copilot-setup-steps.yml configuration, preinstalling tools and dependencies, runners, and settings.

4. //! Bounded LRU cache backed by `BTreeMap`.
5. //!
6. //! Entries are stored in a `BTreeMap` keyed by a caller-chosen type `K` that
7. //! implements `Ord + Clone`. A monotonic counter tracks access order; on
8. //! eviction the entry with the smallest (oldest) counter value is removed.
9. //! Lookups bump the counter to mark the entry as recently used.
10. //!
11. //! # Capacity
12. //!
13. //! The cache is bounded by a capacity given at construction time. When the
14. //! cache is full, the least-recently-used entry is evicted before inserting a
15. //! new one.
16. //!
17. //! # Example
18. //!
19. //! ```
20. //! use cache::Cache;
21. //!
22. //! let mut cache: Cache<&str, i32> = Cache::new(2);
23. //! cache.put("a", 1);
24. //! cache.put("b", 2);
25. //! assert_eq!(*cache.get(&"a").unwrap(), 1);
26. //!
27. //! // Inserting a third entry evicts "b" (least recently used).
28. //! cache.put("c", 3);
29. //! assert!(cache.get(&"b").is_none());
30. //! assert_eq!(*cache.get(&"c").unwrap(), 3);
31. //! ```

1. # View Design: `cache` (Bounded LRU Cache)
2. 
3. ## Abstract Resource
4. 
5. A **bounded key-value map with LRU eviction**: callers store key-value pairs up
6. to a fixed capacity, and when the cache is full and a new key is inserted, the
7. least-recently-accessed entry is automatically evicted.
8. 
9. ---
10. 
11. ## View Struct
12. 
13. ```rust
14. pub struct CacheView<K, V> {
15.     /// The key-value mapping of all cached entries.
16.     pub contents: Map<K, V>,
17.     /// Maximum number of entries the cache can hold.
18.     pub capacity: nat,
19.     /// Keys ordered from least-recently-used (index 0) to most-recently-used (last).
20.     pub lru_order: Seq<K>,
21. }
22. ```
23. 
24. ### Abstraction pattern
25. 
26. **Ghost Struct View + wf()** — the View is a mathematical model of the cache's
27. caller-visible state, using `Map`, `Seq`, and `nat` instead of machine types.
28. 
29. ---
30. 
31. ## Well-formedness Invariant
32. 
33. ```rust
34. impl<K, V> CacheView<K, V> {
35.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
36.         // 1. Size never exceeds the configured capacity.
37.         &&& self.contents.dom().len() <= self.capacity
38.         // 2. LRU order contains exactly the stored keys, without duplicates.
39.         &&& self.lru_order.no_duplicates()
40.         &&& self.lru_order.to_set() == self.contents.dom()
41.         // 3. Explicit cardinality link (derivable from 2, but helps the solver).
42.         &&& self.lru_order.len() == self.contents.dom().len()
43.     }
44. }
45. ```
46. 
47. ### Invariant clauses explained
48. 
49. | # | Clause | Purpose |
50. |---|--------|---------|
51. | 1 | `contents.dom().len() <= capacity` | Capacity bound — the core size constraint callers depend on. |
52. | 2 | `no_duplicates() ∧ to_set() == dom()` | The LRU sequence is a permutation of the key set — every key appears exactly once, and every stored key has a position. |
53. | 3 | `lru_order.len() == contents.dom().len()` | Explicit length link. Derivable from (2), but stated for SMT convenience: needed when proving `lru_order[0]` is safe in the eviction branch. |
54. 
55. ---
56. 
57. ## Helper Spec Function
58. 
59. ```rust
60. impl<K, V> CacheView<K, V> {
61.     /// Move `key` to the most-recently-used position (end of the sequence).
62.     /// Preserves all other elements and their relative order.
63.     pub open spec fn move_to_mru(self, key: K) -> Seq<K> {
64.         self.lru_order.filter(|k: K| k != key).push(key)
65.     }
66. }
67. ```
68. 
69. This helper isolates the `filter(…).push(…)` pattern so that properties
70. (set-preservation, no-duplicates preservation, last-element identity) can be
71. proved once as lemmas and reused across `spec_get` and `spec_put`.
72. 
73. ---
74. 
75. ## Spec Transition Functions
76. 
77. All transitions have the implicit precondition `recommends self.inv()`.
78. 
79. ### `spec_new`
80. 
81. ```rust
82. pub open spec fn spec_new(capacity: nat) -> CacheView<K, V> {
83.     CacheView {
84.         contents: Map::empty(),
85.         capacity,
86.         lru_order: Seq::empty(),
87.     }
88. }
89. ```
90. 
91. ### `spec_get`
92. 
93. Returns the updated cache state and the lookup result.
94. 
95. ```rust
96. pub open spec fn spec_get(self, key: K) -> (CacheView<K, V>, Option<V>) {
97.     if self.contents.dom().contains(key) {
98.         (CacheView {
99.             lru_order: self.move_to_mru(key),
100.             ..self

100.             ..self
101.         }, Some(self.contents[key]))
102.     } else {
103.         (self, None)
104.     }
105. }
106. ```
107. 
108. - **Hit:** recency is refreshed (key moves to MRU); contents and capacity
109.   unchanged.  Returns `Some(value)`.
110. - **Miss:** state unchanged.  Returns `None`.
111. 
112. ### `spec_put`
113. 
114. ```rust
115. pub open spec fn spec_put(self, key: K, value: V) -> CacheView<K, V> {
116.     if self.capacity == 0 {
117.         // Zero-capacity cache: no-op.
118.         self
119.     } else if self.contents.dom().contains(key) {
120.         // Overwrite existing key: replace value, refresh recency.
121.         CacheView {
122.             contents: self.contents.insert(key, value),
123.             lru_order: self.move_to_mru(key),
124.             ..self
125.         }
126.     } else if self.contents.dom().len() >= self.capacity {
127.         // At capacity with new key: evict LRU victim, then insert.
128.         let victim = self.lru_order[0];
129.         CacheView {
130.             contents: self.contents.remove(victim).insert(key, value),
131.             lru_order: self.lru_order.subrange(1, self.lru_order.len() as int).push(key),
132.             ..self
133.         }
134.     } else {
135.         // Below capacity with new key: insert directly.
136.         CacheView {
137.             contents: self.contents.insert(key, value),
138.             lru_order: self.lru_order.push(key),
139.             ..self
140.         }
141.     }
142. }
143. ```
144. 
145. - **Eviction safety:** the branch `contents.dom().len() >= capacity` with
146.   `capacity > 0` plus `inv()` guarantees `lru_order.len() >= 1`, so
147.   `lru_order[0]` is well-defined.
148. 
149. ### `spec_remove`
150. 
151. ```rust
152. pub open spec fn spec_remove(self, key: K) -> CacheView<K, V> {
153.     if self.contents.dom().contains(key) {
154.         CacheView {
155.             contents: self.contents.remove(key),
156.             lru_order: self.lru_order.filter(|k: K| k != key),
157.             ..self
158.         }
159.     } else {
160.         // Key absent: no-op.
161.         self
162.     }
163. }
164. ```
165. 
166. ### `spec_clear`
167. 
168. ```rust
169. pub open spec fn spec_clear(self) -> CacheView<K, V> {
170.     CacheView {
171.         contents: Map::empty(),
172.         lru_order: Seq::empty(),
173.         ..self  // capacity preserved
174.     }
175. }
176. ```
177.

179. 
180. ## CacheGuard Modeling
181. 
182. `CacheGuard<'_, V>` implements `Deref<Target=V>` and `DerefMut`.  It is a
183. transparent borrow wrapper over `&mut V` — the value stored inside the cache.
184. 
185. **Design decision: no separate GuardView type.**
186. 
187. Rationale:
188. 
189. 1. **The guard is a thin smart pointer.**  Its only abstract state is the value
190.    it dereferences to.  A `GuardView<V>` would contain a single field `value: V`
191.    — isomorphic to `V` itself, adding no information.
192. 
193. 2. **Verus handles `&mut` natively.**  When `get(&mut self)` returns a
194.    `CacheGuard<'_, V>`, Verus tracks the mutable borrow.  While the guard is
195.    live the cache is exclusively borrowed; when the guard is dropped, any
196.    mutations to `*guard` are reflected in the cache's post-state.  This is
197.    standard `&mut` semantics, not a cache-specific concern.
198. 
199. 3. **Spec-phase guidance:**
200.    - The `get` ensures clause will state `*result == old(self)@.contents[key]`

387. 
388. ### MOD-1: Capacity Bound Maintenance
389. 
390. **Statement:** After every public operation, `self@.contents.dom().len() <= self@.capacity`.
391.

405. - `remove`: `self.counter == old(self).counter`
406. - `clear`: `self.counter == 0` (reset, but acceptable since entries are also cleared)

418.

1. # Trust Boundary Audit — libs/cache
2. 
3. This file documents all trust items (external_body, admit, external_type_specification)
4. used in the cache crate verification.
5. 
6. ## Root Cause
7. 
8. vstd provides BTreeMap specifications in `vstd::std_specs::btree` (View trait,
9. `assume_specification` for `new`, `insert`, `get`, `remove`, `clear`, `len`, `iter`,
10. `contains_key`, `keys`, `values`). However, the btree module is gated behind
11. `cfg(all(feature = "alloc", feature = "std"))` and internally imports from
12. `std::collections`, making it structurally incompatible with this crate's `no_std`
13. kernel target (`-Z build-std=core,alloc,compiler_builtins`). Enabling the `std`
14. feature is not possible because the `std` crate does not exist on the i686-nanvix
15. kernel target.
16. 
17. To work around this, `lib.vstd_btree.rs` provides equivalent
18. `assume_specification` declarations for `alloc::collections::BTreeMap` methods
19. (`new`, `insert`, `len`, `is_empty`, `clear`) and an uninterpreted
20. `btreemap_view_spec` function instead of `impl View for BTreeMap`.
21. 
22. Additionally, `BTreeMap::get_mut` (used by `Cache::get` and `Cache::put`) has no
23. vstd spec even in the `std` btree module, and returns `Option<&mut V>` — a Verus
24. limitation on `&mut` return types.
25. 
26. `CacheGuard` contains `&'a mut V` which Verus cannot handle in struct
27. fields ("The verifier does not yet support &mut types, except in special cases").
28. 
29. ## External Type Specifications
30. 
31. ### ExBTreeMap — `lib.vstd_btree.rs:31-38`
32. - **Trust item:** `external_type_specification` + `external_body`
33. - **Classification:** `EXTERNAL_TYPE`
34. - **Reason:** `alloc::collections::BTreeMap` is not in vstd on no_std targets.
35.   Verus requires a type declaration to reference it in verified structs.
36.   `external_body` is needed because BTreeMap has private fields.
37. - **Reproducer:** Any `#[verus_verify]` struct containing `BTreeMap<K, V>` fails with
38.   "cannot use type `alloc::collections::BTreeMap` which is ignored because it is either
39.   declared outside the verus! macro or it is marked as `external`."
40. 
41. ### ExGlobal — `lib.vstd_btree.rs:40-41`
42. - **Trust item:** `external_type_specification`
43. - **Classification:** `EXTERNAL_TYPE`
44. - **Reason:** `alloc::alloc::Global` is the default allocator for `BTreeMap<K, V>`.
45.   Declaring BTreeMap requires this type to be visible to Verus.
46. 
47. ### ExCacheEntry — `lib.spec.rs:17-18`
48. - **Trust item:** `external_type_specification`
49. - **Classification:** `EXTERNAL_TYPE`
50. - **Reason:** `CacheEntry<V>` is a private struct used as the value type in
51.   `BTreeMap<K, CacheEntry<V>>`. Verus needs to see it to verify Cache.
52. 
53. ### ExCacheGuard — `lib.spec.rs:23-25`
54. - **Trust item:** `external_type_specification` + `external_body`
55. - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
56. - **Reason:** `CacheGuard<'a, V>` has field `value: &'a mut V`. Verus does not
57.   support `&mut` in struct field types. `external_body` hides the struct fields.
58. - **Reproducer:** Adding `#[verus_verify]` to `CacheGuard` produces
59.   "The verifier does not yet support &mut types, except in special cases".
60. 
61. ## external_body Functions
62. 
63. ### btreemap_remove — `lib.rs:114-123`
64. - **Trust item:** `external_body`
65. - **Classification:** `STDLIB_WRAPPER`
66. - **Reason:** `BTreeMap::remove()` has a `Borrow<Q>` generic parameter that
67.   cannot be monomorphized in `assume_specification` for
68.   `alloc::collections::BTreeMap`. This thin wrapper fixes Q=K and provides
69.   pre/post conditions. Body is a single stdlib call.
70. - **Spec:** `btreemap_view_spec(*m) == old(*m).remove(*k)`, returns the removed
71.   value if present.
72. 
73. ### CacheGuard::deref — `lib.rs:93-99`
74. - **Trust item:** `external_body`
75. - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
76. - **Reason:** CacheGuard is `external_body` (Verus cannot see `&mut V` field).
77.   The body `self.value` accesses the opaque field.
78. - **Spec:** `*ret == self@` — dereferencing yields the guard's abstract value.
79. 
80. ### Cache::get — `lib.rs:190-218`
81. - **Trust item:** `external_body`
82. - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
83. - **Reason:** Body calls `BTreeMap::get_mut()` which (a) has no vstd spec even
84.   in the `std` btree module, and (b) returns `Option<&mut V>` — a Verus `&mut`
85.   return type limitation. Also constructs `CacheGuard` with `&mut`.
86. - **Spec:** On hit: `result is Some`, guard view equals `spec_get(*key).1.unwrap()`,
87.   state transitions via `spec_get`. On miss: `result is None`, view unchanged.
88. 
89. ### Cache::put — `lib.rs:230-265`
90. - **Trust item:** `external_body`
91. - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
92. - **Reason:** Same `get_mut` blockers as Cache::get (no vstd spec, `&mut` return
93.   type). Rewriting to avoid `get_mut` would change the existing-key path from
94.   in-place mutation to a `remove` + `insert` sequence — a structural exec code
95.   modification violating source integrity. The `contains_key` alternative also
96.   has the `Borrow<Q>` blocker (same as `remove`).
97. - **Spec:** `self@ == old(self)@.spec_put(key, value)`, invariant preserved.
98. 
99. ### Cache::evict — `lib.rs:321-344`
100. - **Trust item:** `external_body`
101. - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
102. - **Reason:** Uses `self.entries.iter().min_by_key(|(_, e)| e.last_used)`
103.   iterator chain with closure, plus `BTreeMap::remove()`. Iterator combinators
104.   (`iter`, `min_by_key`, `map`) have no vstd specs.
105. - **Spec:** LRU victim (`lru_order[0]`) evicted, contents/order updated accordingly.
106. 
107. ### axiom_cache_lru_of_remove — `lib.proof.rs:408-418`
108. - **Trust item:** `external_body` (on proof fn)
109. - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
110. - **Reason:** Axiom relating the uninterpreted `cache_lru_of` function to
111.   BTreeMap removal. `cache_lru_of` is partially uninterpreted (uses
112.   `cache_lru_of_nonempty` for non-empty maps) because the concrete LRU
113.   ordering depends on `CacheEntry::last_used` counter values, which cannot
114.   be expressed as a closed-form spec function over `BTreeMap` entries.
115.   Sound because `BTreeMap::remove` does not change `last_used` counters of
116.   remaining entries, so their relative sort order is preserved.
117. - **Spec:** `cache_lru_of(new) == cache_lru_of(old).filter(|k| k != key)`.
118. 
119. ## Body-Verified Functions
120. 
121. The following functions are verified without `external_body`:
122. 
123. | Function | Status |
124. |---|---|
125. | `Cache::new` | ✅ Body verified (calls `BTreeMap::new` with local `assume_specification`) |
126. | `Cache::remove` | ✅ Body verified (uses `btreemap_remove` wrapper + `axiom_cache_lru_of_remove`) |
127. | `Cache::clear` | ✅ Body verified (calls `BTreeMap::clear` with local `assume_specification`) |
128. 
129. ## Unverifiable Functions
130. 
131. ### CacheGuard::deref_mut — `lib.rs:102-105`
132. - **Trust item:** No spec (function excluded from verification)
133. - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
134. - **Reason:** `deref_mut` returns `&mut V`. Verus error: "The verifier does not
135.   yet support &mut types, except in special cases" (on the function signature).
136.   The function cannot have any spec annotation at all.
137. - **Reproducer:** Adding `#[verus_verify(external_body)]` to `deref_mut` produces
138.   the `&mut` type error.
139. - **Impact:** Mutation-through-guard semantics are unmodeled. Callers who mutate
140.   a value through `*guard = new_value` have no formal guarantee the change
141.   persists in the cache. This is documented but cannot be resolved until Verus
142.   adds `&mut` return type support.
143. 
144. ## Trust Assumptions
145. 
146. ### Counter overflow — `lib.rs:210,246`
147. - **Assumption:** `self.counter` (type `u64`) never overflows during the
148.   lifetime of a Cache instance.
149. - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION` (precondition omitted)
150. - **Justification:** At 10 billion ops/sec, overflow requires ~58 years.
151.   Physically unreachable. Adding `requires self.counter < u64::MAX` would
152.   burden every caller with a practically-impossible proof obligation.
153. - **See also:** `bugs.md` BUG-1.
154. 
155. ## admit() in Proof Stubs
156. 
157. All five admit() placeholders have been eliminated. The invariant preservation
158. lemmas are now fully proven:
159. 
160. | Lemma | Status |
161. |---|---|
162. | `lemma_spec_new_inv` | ✅ Proven |
163. | `lemma_spec_get_inv` | ✅ Proven |
164. | `lemma_spec_put_inv` | ✅ Proven |
165. | `lemma_spec_remove_inv` | ✅ Proven |
166. | `lemma_spec_clear_inv` | ✅ Proven |
167. 
168. ## assume_specification Items (lib.vstd_btree.rs)

 # Trust Boundary Audit — libs/cache
 
 This file documents all trust items (external_body, admit, external_type_specification)
 used in the cache crate verification.
 
 ## Root Cause
 
 vstd provides BTreeMap specifications in `vstd::std_specs::btree` (View trait,
 `assume_specification` for `new`, `insert`, `get`, `remove`, `clear`, `len`, `iter`,
 `contains_key`, `keys`, `values`). However, the btree module is gated behind
 `cfg(all(feature = "alloc", feature = "std"))` and internally imports from
 `std::collections`, making it structurally incompatible with this crate's `no_std`
 kernel target (`-Z build-std=core,alloc,compiler_builtins`). Enabling the `std`
 feature is not possible because the `std` crate does not exist on the i686-nanvix
 kernel target.
 
 To work around this, `lib.vstd_btree.rs` provides equivalent
 `assume_specification` declarations for `alloc::collections::BTreeMap` methods
 (`new`, `insert`, `len`, `is_empty`, `clear`) and an uninterpreted
 `btreemap_view_spec` function instead of `impl View for BTreeMap`.
 
 Additionally, `BTreeMap::get_mut` (used by `Cache::get` and `Cache::put`) has no
 vstd spec even in the `std` btree module, and returns `Option<&mut V>` — a Verus
 limitation on `&mut` return types.
 
 `CacheGuard` contains `&'a mut V` which Verus cannot handle in struct
 fields ("The verifier does not yet support &mut types, except in special cases").
 
 ## External Type Specifications
 
 ### ExBTreeMap — `lib.vstd_btree.rs:31-38`
 - **Trust item:** `external_type_specification` + `external_body`
 - **Classification:** `EXTERNAL_TYPE`
 - **Reason:** `alloc::collections::BTreeMap` is not in vstd on no_std targets.
   Verus requires a type declaration to reference it in verified structs.
   `external_body` is needed because BTreeMap has private fields.
 - **Reproducer:** Any `#[verus_verify]` struct containing `BTreeMap<K, V>` fails with
   "cannot use type `alloc::collections::BTreeMap` which is ignored because it is either
   declared outside the verus! macro or it is marked as `external`."
 
 ### ExGlobal — `lib.vstd_btree.rs:40-41`
 - **Trust item:** `external_type_specification`
 - **Classification:** `EXTERNAL_TYPE`
 - **Reason:** `alloc::alloc::Global` is the default allocator for `BTreeMap<K, V>`.
   Declaring BTreeMap requires this type to be visible to Verus.
 
 ### ExCacheEntry — `lib.spec.rs:17-18`
 - **Trust item:** `external_type_specification`
 - **Classification:** `EXTERNAL_TYPE`
 - **Reason:** `CacheEntry<V>` is a private struct used as the value type in
   `BTreeMap<K, CacheEntry<V>>`. Verus needs to see it to verify Cache.
 
 ### ExCacheGuard — `lib.spec.rs:23-25`
 - **Trust item:** `external_type_specification` + `external_body`
 - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
 - **Reason:** `CacheGuard<'a, V>` has field `value: &'a mut V`. Verus does not
   support `&mut` in struct field types. `external_body` hides the struct fields.
 - **Reproducer:** Adding `#[verus_verify]` to `CacheGuard` produces
   "The verifier does not yet support &mut types, except in special cases".
 
 ## external_body Functions
 
 ### btreemap_remove — `lib.rs:114-123`
 - **Trust item:** `external_body`
 - **Classification:** `STDLIB_WRAPPER`
 - **Reason:** `BTreeMap::remove()` has a `Borrow<Q>` generic parameter that
   cannot be monomorphized in `assume_specification` for
   `alloc::collections::BTreeMap`. This thin wrapper fixes Q=K and provides
   pre/post conditions. Body is a single stdlib call.
 - **Spec:** `btreemap_view_spec(*m) == old(*m).remove(*k)`, returns the removed
   value if present.
 
 ### CacheGuard::deref — `lib.rs:93-99`
 - **Trust item:** `external_body`
 - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
 - **Reason:** CacheGuard is `external_body` (Verus cannot see `&mut V` field).
   The body `self.value` accesses the opaque field.
 - **Spec:** `*ret == self@` — dereferencing yields the guard's abstract value.
 
 ### Cache::get — `lib.rs:190-218`
 - **Trust item:** `external_body`
 - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
 - **Reason:** Body calls `BTreeMap::get_mut()` which (a) has no vstd spec even
   in the `std` btree module, and (b) returns `Option<&mut V>` — a Verus `&mut`
   return type limitation. Also constructs `CacheGuard` with `&mut`.
 - **Spec:** On hit: `result is Some`, guard view equals `spec_get(*key).1.unwrap()`,
   state transitions via `spec_get`. On miss: `result is None`, view unchanged.
 
 ### Cache::put — `lib.rs:230-265`
 - **Trust item:** `external_body`
 - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
 - **Reason:** Same `get_mut` blockers as Cache::get (no vstd spec, `&mut` return
   type). Rewriting to avoid `get_mut` would change the existing-key path from
   in-place mutation to a `remove` + `insert` sequence — a structural exec code
   modification violating source integrity. The `contains_key` alternative also
   has the `Borrow<Q>` blocker (same as `remove`).
 - **Spec:** `self@ == old(self)@.spec_put(key, value)`, invariant preserved.
 
 ### Cache::evict — `lib.rs:321-344`
 - **Trust item:** `external_body`
 - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
 - **Reason:** Uses `self.entries.iter().min_by_key(|(_, e)| e.last_used)`
   iterator chain with closure, plus `BTreeMap::remove()`. Iterator combinators
   (`iter`, `min_by_key`, `map`) have no vstd specs.
 - **Spec:** LRU victim (`lru_order[0]`) evicted, contents/order updated accordingly.
 
 ### axiom_cache_lru_of_remove — `lib.proof.rs:408-418`
 - **Trust item:** `external_body` (on proof fn)
 - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
 - **Reason:** Axiom relating the uninterpreted `cache_lru_of` function to
   BTreeMap removal. `cache_lru_of` is partially uninterpreted (uses
   `cache_lru_of_nonempty` for non-empty maps) because the concrete LRU
   ordering depends on `CacheEntry::last_used` counter values, which cannot
   be expressed as a closed-form spec function over `BTreeMap` entries.
   Sound because `BTreeMap::remove` does not change `last_used` counters of
   remaining entries, so their relative sort order is preserved.
 - **Spec:** `cache_lru_of(new) == cache_lru_of(old).filter(|k| k != key)`.

 The following functions are verified without `external_body`:
 
 | Function | Status |
 |---|---|
 | `Cache::new` | ✅ Body verified (calls `BTreeMap::new` with local `assume_specification`) |
 | `Cache::remove` | ✅ Body verified (uses `btreemap_remove` wrapper + `axiom_cache_lru_of_remove`) |
 | `Cache::clear` | ✅ Body verified (calls `BTreeMap::clear` with local `assume_specification`) |
 
 ## Unverifiable Functions
 
 ### CacheGuard::deref_mut — `lib.rs:102-105`
 - **Trust item:** No spec (function excluded from verification)
 - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
 - **Reason:** `deref_mut` returns `&mut V`. Verus error: "The verifier does not
   yet support &mut types, except in special cases" (on the function signature).
   The function cannot have any spec annotation at all.
 - **Reproducer:** Adding `#[verus_verify(external_body)]` to `deref_mut` produces
   the `&mut` type error.
 - **Impact:** Mutation-through-guard semantics are unmodeled. Callers who mutate
   a value through `*guard = new_value` have no formal guarantee the change
   persists in the cache. This is documented but cannot be resolved until Verus
   adds `&mut` return type support.
 
 ## Trust Assumptions
 
 ### Counter overflow — `lib.rs:210,246`
 - **Assumption:** `self.counter` (type `u64`) never overflows during the
   lifetime of a Cache instance.
 - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION` (precondition omitted)
 - **Justification:** At 10 billion ops/sec, overflow requires ~58 years.
   Physically unreachable. Adding `requires self.counter < u64::MAX` would
   burden every caller with a practically-impossible proof obligation.
 - **See also:** `bugs.md` BUG-1.

3. ## BUG-1: Counter overflow (u64)
4. 
5. - **Status:** UNCONFIRMED
6. - **Severity:** LOW (physically unreachable)
7. - **Location:** `lib.rs` — `Cache::get` (line ~192) and `Cache::put` (line ~224)
8. - **Description:** The `counter: u64` field is incremented on every `get` hit and
9.   `put` call without overflow checking (`self.counter += 1`). After 2^64
10.   operations the counter wraps to 0, which would corrupt LRU ordering —
11.   freshly accessed entries would have a lower counter than old ones, causing
12.   incorrect eviction.
13. - **Impact:** At 10 billion ops/sec, overflow requires ~58 years of continuous
14.   operation. Physically unreachable in practice, but the spec does not model
15.   this assumption.
16. - **Spec gap:** No `requires self.counter < u64::MAX` precondition exists.
17.   The spec transition functions use abstract `Seq` ordering (not counters),
18.   so the spec is correct even if the implementation overflows — but the
19.   `external_body` trust gap means the implementation's correctness depends
20.   on no overflow occurring.
21. - **Recommendation:** Document as a trust assumption. Optionally add
22.   `debug_assert!(self.counter < u64::MAX)` or use `checked_add`.

201.      (value identity on return).
202.    - The recency update (`move_to_mru`) is captured in `self@` vs `old(self)@`.

208. ## Design Rationale
209. 
210. ### Field: `contents: Map<K, V>`
211. 
212. - **What it represents:** the set of key-value pairs currently stored.
213. - **Substitution test:** ✅ — any cache implementation, regardless of backing
214.   data structure (hash map, B-tree, array, linked list), maintains a logical
215.   key-value mapping.
216. - **Used in:** every spec transition (get, put, remove, clear) and `inv()`.
217. 
218. ### Field: `capacity: nat`
219. 
220. - **What it represents:** the upper bound on the number of entries.
221. - **Substitution test:** ✅ — any bounded cache has a configurable capacity.
222.   Using `nat` (not `usize`) avoids unnecessary overflow reasoning in specs.
223. - **Used in:** `inv()` (capacity bound) and `spec_put` (eviction decision).
224. 
225. ### Field: `lru_order: Seq<K>`
226. 
227. - **What it represents:** the recency ordering of all cached keys, from
228.   least-recently-used (index 0) to most-recently-used (last element).
229. - **Substitution test:** ✅ — any LRU cache must maintain a total recency
230.   order over its entries, regardless of whether the implementation uses
231.   counters, linked lists, timestamps, or something else.  The ordering is
232.   directly observable through eviction behavior: callers can determine which
233.   entry will be evicted next.
234. - **Used in:** `spec_get` (recency refresh), `spec_put` (eviction victim
235.   selection, recency refresh on overwrite), `spec_remove` (key removal from
236.   order), `spec_clear` (reset), and `inv()`.
237. 
238. ---
239. 
240. ## Rejected Alternatives
241. 
242. ### 1. `recency: Map<K, nat>` instead of `lru_order: Seq<K>`
243. 
244. Map each key to a recency rank (higher = more recent).
245. 
246. **Rejected because:**
247. - Introduces arbitrary counter values that mirror the implementation's internal
248.   counter, violating the substitution test.
249. - Requires additional `inv()` clauses: injectivity (no two keys share a rank),
250.   density or boundedness of ranks, and well-ordering.
251. - Eviction becomes `argmin(recency)` rather than the simpler `lru_order[0]`.
252. - Strictly more complex with no gain in expressiveness.
253. 
254. ### 2. `size: nat` as a separate field
255. 
256. Track the current number of entries explicitly.
257. 
258. **Rejected because:**
259. - Derivable from `contents.dom().len()`.  Adding it violates minimality and
260.   creates a consistency obligation (`size == contents.dom().len()`) in every
261.   transition.
262. 
263. ### 3. `last_accessed: Option<K>` — most-recently-used key
264. 
265. **Rejected because:**

 ## Design Rationale
 
 ### Field: `contents: Map<K, V>`
 
 - **What it represents:** the set of key-value pairs currently stored.
 - **Substitution test:** ✅ — any cache implementation, regardless of backing
   data structure (hash map, B-tree, array, linked list), maintains a logical
   key-value mapping.
 - **Used in:** every spec transition (get, put, remove, clear) and `inv()`.
 
 ### Field: `capacity: nat`
 
 - **What it represents:** the upper bound on the number of entries.
 - **Substitution test:** ✅ — any bounded cache has a configurable capacity.
   Using `nat` (not `usize`) avoids unnecessary overflow reasoning in specs.
 - **Used in:** `inv()` (capacity bound) and `spec_put` (eviction decision).
 
 ### Field: `lru_order: Seq<K>`
 
 - **What it represents:** the recency ordering of all cached keys, from
   least-recently-used (index 0) to most-recently-used (last element).
 - **Substitution test:** ✅ — any LRU cache must maintain a total recency
   order over its entries, regardless of whether the implementation uses
   counters, linked lists, timestamps, or something else.  The ordering is
   directly observable through eviction behavior: callers can determine which
   entry will be evicted next.
 - **Used in:** `spec_get` (recency refresh), `spec_put` (eviction victim
   selection, recency refresh on overwrite), `spec_remove` (key removal from
   order), `spec_clear` (reset), and `inv()`.

 Map each key to a recency rank (higher = more recent).

 - Introduces arbitrary counter values that mirror the implementation's internal
   counter, violating the substitution test.
 - Requires additional `inv()` clauses: injectivity (no two keys share a rank),
   density or boundedness of ranks, and well-ordering.
 - Eviction becomes `argmin(recency)` rather than the simpler `lru_order[0]`.
 - Strictly more complex with no gain in expressiveness.
 
 ### 2. `size: nat` as a separate field
 
 Track the current number of entries explicitly.
 
 **Rejected because:**
 - Derivable from `contents.dom().len()`.  Adding it violates minimality and
   creates a consistency obligation (`size == contents.dom().len()`) in every
   transition.
 
 ### 3. `last_accessed: Option<K>` — most-recently-used key
 
 **Rejected because:**
 - Subsume by `lru_order.last()`.  Adding it violates minimality.
 
 ### 4. No `lru_order` field (just `contents` + `capacity`)
 
 **Rejected because:**
 - Under-specified: without the ordering, we cannot specify *which* entry is

 **Rejected because:**

name: verus-constraints
description: "Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code."
---

# Verus Constraints

Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/` for a complete example following all
constraints below.

## Attribute Style for Exec Functions

All specs on **exec functions** must use the attribute-based syntax
(`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`).
See the **verus-syntax** skill for the full reference and examples.

```rust
// ✅ CORRECT — attribute style for exec functions
#[verus_spec(ret =>
    requires x < 100,
    ensures ret == x + 1,
)]
fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 {
    x + 1
}

// ❌ WRONG — do not wrap exec functions in verus! { }
verus! {
    fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
        requires x < 100,
        ensures ret == x + 1,
    { x + 1 }
} // verus!
```

**`verus! { }` blocks** are still used for:
- `spec fn` and `proof fn` definitions (in `.spec.rs` and `.proof.rs`)
- Type-level specs (`broadcast`, `impl View`, etc.)

Key benefit: exec function signatures stay unmodified — the original `fn`
signature is untouched, specs live in the attribute.

## Source Integrity (exec code)

The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
`*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.

Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Keep changes
minimal so developers can review diffs easily.

**Preserve by default:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions,
comments, debug assertions, and all other existing code.

**Minimal equivalent rewrites** are allowed when Verus genuinely cannot express
a construct. The escalation ladder (each step requires exhausting the previous):

1. **Verify as-is** — most code works with Verus directly.
2. **Search vstd** — your training data is likely outdated. `grep -r` the entire
   vstd directory. Check `std_specs/`, recent additions.
3. **Minimal equivalent rewrite** — rewrite the smallest possible expression
   to an equivalent one Verus accepts. Requirements:
   - Same semantics (identical observable behavior for all inputs)
   - Same panic/error behavior
   - Same asymptotic time and space complexity
   - Smallest possible diff
   - `// VERUS REWRITE: <reason>` comment on the changed code
   - Minimal reproducer proving the original is unsupported
4. **Stdlib wrapper** — if a stdlib/core function call fails because Verus
   cannot handle the parameter types (e.g., `&mut [T]` from `DerefMut`
   coercion, closures), create a thin wrapper function whose body contains
   **ONLY** the stdlib call. Mark the wrapper `external_body` with pre/post
   conditions. The original function calls the wrapper instead. This isolates
   the trust boundary to the thinnest possible layer.

   Example — `core::mem::replace` on `&mut Vec<T>[index]`:
   ```rust
   #[verus_verify(external_body)]
   #[verus_spec(prev =>
       requires index < old(v)@.len(),
       ensures
           prev == old(v)@[index as int],
           v@ == old(v)@.update(index as int, value),
           v@.len() == old(v)@.len(),
   )]
   fn vec_replace<T>(v: &mut Vec<T>, index: usize, value: T) -> T {
       ::core::mem::replace(&mut v[index], value)
   }
   ```
   The wrapper body is a single stdlib call. The `external_body` trusts only
   this one line. The calling function remains fully body-verified.

5. **`external_body` on the original** — absolute last resort. Requires a
   minimal reproducer and `trust.md` entry.

**Principle:** prefer rewriting code to a semantic equivalent over ANY cheating.
A rewrite that lets Verus verify the body is always better than `external_body`.

**Never cfg-gate away and duplicate exec definitions.** Adding
`#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to a function, impl block, struct, enum, or
constant and providing a verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the
copy, not the real code, and the two will silently diverge.

- **Functions / impl blocks**: add contracts to the original in-place.
- **Structs / enums**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If a
  derive macro is incompatible, cfg-gate only the derive attribute, not
  the struct. If the struct truly cannot be parsed by Verus, use
  `external_type_specification` in spec.rs to declare it — do not
  duplicate the definition.
- **Constants**: if the initializer uses only literals and Verus-visible
  symbols, Verus sees it directly — no duplication needed. If it references
  external symbols Verus cannot resolve (e.g. `mem::PAGE_SIZE`), add a
  spec duplicate inside `verus! {}` under `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]` with
  the literal value — but keep the original **ungated** so exec code still
  uses it. Never `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` the original constant.

**Allowed additions:** `#[verus_spec(...)]` and `#[verus_verify]` attributes,
`proof! { }` / `proof_decl! { }` / `proof_with! { }` macros, `#[verus_spec(...)]`
on loops, `verus! { }` blocks (for spec/proof fn in .spec.rs/.proof.rs),
vstd imports (cfg-gated), ghost/tracked local variables (each must be
used by at least one proof construct — assertion, invariant, or proof block),
`Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` struct fields (only when proof requires ghost
state to flow through exec code — prefer keeping ghost state in View),
`#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]` gating.

**After completing all changes**, use the `ast-consistency` skill to verify
source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies. For unavoidable ones, you must
confirm: (1) the code still builds with `cargo build`, (2) semantic code logic
is unchanged, (3) it is a genuine Verus limitation, and (4) it is documented
in `trust.md`.

## Forbidden Patterns

| Pattern | Policy |
|---|---|
| `admit()` | Banned — only as placeholder in specification phase (must be eliminated in proving) |
| `assume(...)` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external_body]` | Last resort — requires exhausting the escalation ladder (verify as-is → vstd search → minimal rewrite → stdlib wrapper). Must have minimal reproducer and `trust.md` entry |
| `#[verifier::trusted]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external]` | Banned — do not use to "fix" verification errors |
| `#[verifier::exec_allows_no_decreases_clause]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::rlimit(N)]` | Timeout means the proof is too weak — simplify the proof, split lemmas, add intermediate assertions. Never use rlimit to work around timeouts. If all proof strategies are exhausted and the proof is genuinely optimal, rlimit up to 50 is the absolute maximum |
| `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` on exec code | **Cheating** — cfg-gating branches, expressions, match arms, or code blocks means Verus verifies different code than what runs. Only allowed on non-semantic items: `derive(...)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`), and imports |

## trust.md

Any use of the following MUST be documented in `trust.md` (in the logs directory):
- `external_body` on any function
- `admit()` remaining after proving phase
- `assume(...)` anywhere
- `cfg-gated exec code` (beyond imports/derives/logging)
- `assume_specification` or `axiom`

Each entry must include:
1. Function name and file:line location
2. What trust item was used
3. Minimal reproducer proving it cannot be avoided
4. Classification: `STDLIB_WRAPPER` / `VERUS_LIMITATION` / `EXTERNAL_TYPE` / `TEMPORARY`

`trust.md` is an **audit log**, not approval. Items classified `TEMPORARY`
are blockers that must be resolved. Items with no reproducer are blockers.

## assume_specification

`assume_specification` provides specs for std library or external functions
whose body Verus cannot verify (because vstd does not include them).
These are **external-bottom** trust assumptions (see **spec-design** skill) —
unverified axioms that, if wrong, make downstream proofs unsound.

**Allowed** for std library / external functions not covered by vstd.
Follow the audit checklist in `spec-design` (documentation fidelity, soft
contract coverage, no stronger than the API, version sensitivity).

**Before writing:** search vstd for existing specs of that function,
search verified dependency specs for reusable `assume_specification`,
look for safe Verus API alternatives, try restructuring to avoid the call.

**`axiom` requires human approval** — it introduces arbitrary unverified
axioms with no connection to an external API contract.

## vstd & Common Misconceptions

vstd is rapidly evolving — specs you believe are missing may already exist.
**Your training data is likely outdated.** Before concluding that a std
function has no spec or that a construct is unsupported, you **must** search
the actual vstd source thoroughly:

```bash
grep -r "function_name" /path/to/vstd/        # broad search
grep -r "spec.*fn.*method" /path/to/vstd/     # spec function patterns
```

Search broadly across the entire vstd directory — do not only check one or
two files. Look in `vstd/std_specs/`, `vstd/seq*.rs`, `vstd/map*.rs`,
`vstd/set*.rs`, `vstd/arithmetic/`, `vstd/raw_ptr.rs`, etc.

- **Never invent vstd functions** — verify existence in actual vstd source.
- **Verus supports `for` loops** — do not replace with `while` unless semantically appropriate.
- **Don't hallucinate syntax** — when unsure, check the Verus reference or vstd examples.

## Claiming Verus Limitations

**Principle: isolate and test before concluding.** A failing expression is
evidence only about that expression — not about broader language features —
until a smaller isolated reproducer shows the specific construct also fails.

When `f(|x| expr)` fails, the error might be in `f`, in `|x|`, in `expr`,
or in the combination. You **cannot** conclude "closures are unsupported"
from one failed call. You must test each component separately.

**Do not generalize from an unsupported API to a feature class.** If
`v.sort_by_key(|x| x.field)` fails, that is evidence about `sort_by_key` (or
about `&mut` complex args), not about closures. You must isolate and test
the closure by itself before claiming closures are unsupported.

### Required diagnostic steps

Before claiming any construct is unsupported, you **must**:

1. **Read the actual error.** Verus errors are specific — "partition_point is
   not supported" means `partition_point` lacks a spec, not that closures fail.
2. **Isolate the construct.** Write a minimal standalone `.rs` file that tests
   ONLY the construct you suspect is unsupported. **Run it through Verus** and
   quote the actual error. Do not claim "X is unsupported" unless an isolated
   repro for X itself fails.
   - If a closure-taking function fails, test a standalone closure first,
     then test a simpler closure-taking API (e.g., `Option::map`).
   - If a for-loop over an iterator fails, test `for x in vec` first.
3. **Search for counterexamples** in `verus-lang/verus/source/rust_verify_test/tests/`
   and in vstd source. If others use the construct successfully, your problem
   is elsewhere.
4. **Search vstd** — `grep -r` across the entire vstd directory. Check
   `std_specs/` for `assume_specification` on stdlib functions.
5. **Apply an approved workaround** if one matches:
   - `|_|` → `|_e|` (Verus requires named variables in closures)
   - Incompatible derives → `#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]`
   - `debug_assert!` / logging macros → `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` on the statement
6. **Minimal equivalent rewrite** — follow the escalation ladder in Source
   Integrity. Only after isolated repro confirms the specific construct fails.
7. **Stdlib wrapper** — only after isolated repro shows the API call itself
   is the failing unit (see Source Integrity step 4).

### Examples of past false generalizations

| Error on | False conclusion | Reality |
|---|---|---|
| `v.partition_point(\|x\| ...)` | "closures not supported" | `partition_point` lacks vstd spec; closures work fine |
| `v.sort_by_key(\|x\| ...)` | "closures not supported" | `&mut` complex args unsupported; closures work fine |
| `for x in v.windows(2)` | "iterators not supported" | `Windows` lacks `ForLoopGhostIteratorNew`; `for x in vec` works |
| `for i in (0..n).rev()` | "ranges not supported" | `Rev<Range>` lacks trait impl; `for i in 0..n` works |
| `x.ok_or_else(\|\| err)` | "closures not supported" | Works — vstd has `assume_specification` for it |

### Guardrails

**Cfg-gating exec code is cheating.** `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` is only
appropriate for non-semantic items that Verus truly cannot parse:
`derive(Debug)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`).
Do NOT cfg-gate match arms, closures, large code blocks, or expressions.
This makes Verus verify different code than what actually runs.

**Anti-pattern — body duplication (absolutely forbidden):**

```rust
// ❌ WRONG: real body hidden from Verus, replaced with different code
fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> {
    #[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
    { /* real implementation */ }
    #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
    { /* different code that Verus can parse */ }
}
```

**Anti-pattern — function duplication (absolutely forbidden):**

```rust
// ❌ WRONG: entire function gated out, replaced with a different definition
#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* real */ }
#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* different */ }
```

Both patterns verify a **different program** than what ships. The proof is
meaningless. Find a single body that both Rust and Verus accept — or use
`external_body` and document in trust.md.

Partial contracts are always better than none. If 1 out of 5 clauses is
inexpressible, write the other 4.

   ```rust
           v@.len() == old(v)@.len(),
   )]
   fn vec_replace<T>(v: &mut Vec<T>, index: usize, value: T) -> T {
       ::core::mem::replace(&mut v[index], value)
   }
   ```
   The wrapper body is a single stdlib call. The `external_body` trusts only
   this one line. The calling function remains fully body-verified.

5. **`external_body` on the original** — absolute last resort. Requires a
   minimal reproducer and `trust.md` entry.

**Principle:** prefer rewriting code to a semantic equivalent over ANY cheating.
A rewrite that lets Verus verify the body is always better than `external_body`.

**Never cfg-gate away and duplicate exec definitions.** Adding
`#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to a function, impl block, struct, enum, or
constant and providing a verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the
copy, not the real code, and the two will silently diverge.

- **Functions / impl blocks**: add contracts to the original in-place.
- **Structs / enums**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If a
  derive macro is incompatible, cfg-gate only the derive attribute, not
  the struct. If the struct truly cannot be parsed by Verus, use
  `external_type_specification` in spec.rs to declare it — do not
  duplicate the definition.
- **Constants**: if the initializer uses only literals and Verus-visible
  symbols, Verus sees it directly — no duplication needed. If it references
  external symbols Verus cannot resolve (e.g. `mem::PAGE_SIZE`), add a
  spec duplicate inside `verus! {}` under `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]` with
  the literal value — but keep the original **ungated** so exec code still
  uses it. Never `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` the original constant.

**Allowed additions:** `#[verus_spec(...)]` and `#[verus_verify]` attributes,
`proof! { }` / `proof_decl! { }` / `proof_with! { }` macros, `#[verus_spec(...)]`
on loops, `verus! { }` blocks (for spec/proof fn in .spec.rs/.proof.rs),
vstd imports (cfg-gated), ghost/tracked local variables (each must be
used by at least one proof construct — assertion, invariant, or proof block),
`Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` struct fields (only when proof requires ghost
state to flow through exec code — prefer keeping ghost state in View),
`#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]` gating.

**After completing all changes**, use the `ast-consistency` skill to verify
source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies. For unavoidable ones, you must
confirm: (1) the code still builds with `cargo build`, (2) semantic code logic
is unchanged, (3) it is a genuine Verus limitation, and (4) it is documented
in `trust.md`.

## Forbidden Patterns

| Pattern | Policy |
|---|---|
| `admit()` | Banned — only as placeholder in specification phase (must be eliminated in proving) |
| `assume(...)` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external_body]` | Last resort — requires exhausting the escalation ladder (verify as-is → vstd search → minimal rewrite → stdlib wrapper). Must have minimal reproducer and `trust.md` entry |
| `#[verifier::trusted]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external]` | Banned — do not use to "fix" verification errors |
| `#[verifier::exec_allows_no_decreases_clause]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::rlimit(N)]` | Timeout means the proof is too weak — simplify the proof, split lemmas, add intermediate assertions. Never use rlimit to work around timeouts. If all proof strategies are exhausted and the proof is genuinely optimal, rlimit up to 50 is the absolute maximum |
| `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` on exec code | **Cheating** — cfg-gating branches, expressions, match arms, or code blocks means Verus verifies different code than what runs. Only allowed on non-semantic items: `derive(...)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`), and imports |

## trust.md

Any use of the following MUST be documented in `trust.md` (in the logs directory):
- `external_body` on any function
- `admit()` remaining after proving phase
- `assume(...)` anywhere
- `cfg-gated exec code` (beyond imports/derives/logging)
- `assume_specification` or `axiom`

Each entry must include:
1. Function name and file:line location
2. What trust item was used
3. Minimal reproducer proving it cannot be avoided
4. Classification: `STDLIB_WRAPPER` / `VERUS_LIMITATION` / `EXTERNAL_TYPE` / `TEMPORARY`

`trust.md` is an **audit log**, not approval. Items classified `TEMPORARY`
are blockers that must be resolved. Items with no reproducer are blockers.

## assume_specification

`assume_specification` provides specs for std library or external functions
whose body Verus cannot verify (because vstd does not include them).
These are **external-bottom** trust assumptions (see **spec-design** skill) —
unverified axioms that, if wrong, make downstream proofs unsound.

**Allowed** for std library / external functions not covered by vstd.
Follow the audit checklist in `spec-design` (documentation fidelity, soft
contract coverage, no stronger than the API, version sensitivity).

**Before writing:** search vstd for existing specs of that function,
search verified dependency specs for reusable `assume_specification`,
look for safe Verus API alternatives, try restructuring to avoid the call.

**`axiom` requires human approval** — it introduces arbitrary unverified
axioms with no connection to an external API contract.

## vstd & Common Misconceptions

vstd is rapidly evolving — specs you believe are missing may already exist.
**Your training data is likely outdated.** Before concluding that a std
function has no spec or that a construct is unsupported, you **must** search
the actual vstd source thoroughly:

```bash
grep -r "function_name" /path/to/vstd/        # broad search
grep -r "spec.*fn.*method" /path/to/vstd/     # spec function patterns
```

Search broadly across the entire vstd directory — do not only check one or
two files. Look in `vstd/std_specs/`, `vstd/seq*.rs`, `vstd/map*.rs`,
`vstd/set*.rs`, `vstd/arithmetic/`, `vstd/raw_ptr.rs`, etc.

- **Never invent vstd functions** — verify existence in actual vstd source.
- **Verus supports `for` loops** — do not replace with `while` unless semantically appropriate.
- **Don't hallucinate syntax** — when unsure, check the Verus reference or vstd examples.

## Claiming Verus Limitations

**Principle: isolate and test before concluding.** A failing expression is
evidence only about that expression — not about broader language features —
until a smaller isolated reproducer shows the specific construct also fails.

When `f(|x| expr)` fails, the error might be in `f`, in `|x|`, in `expr`,
or in the combination. You **cannot** conclude "closures are unsupported"
from one failed call. You must test each component separately.

**Do not generalize from an unsupported API to a feature class.** If
`v.sort_by_key(|x| x.field)` fails, that is evidence about `sort_by_key` (or
about `&mut` complex args), not about closures. You must isolate and test
the closure by itself before claiming closures are unsupported.

### Required diagnostic steps

Before claiming any construct is unsupported, you **must**:

1. **Read the actual error.** Verus errors are specific — "partition_point is
   not supported" means `partition_point` lacks a spec, not that closures fail.
2. **Isolate the construct.** Write a minimal standalone `.rs` file that tests
   ONLY the construct you suspect is unsupported. **Run it through Verus** and
   quote the actual error. Do not claim "X is unsupported" unless an isolated
   repro for X itself fails.
   - If a closure-taking function fails, test a standalone closure first,
     then test a simpler closure-taking API (e.g., `Option::map`).
   - If a for-loop over an iterator fails, test `for x in vec` first.
3. **Search for counterexamples** in `verus-lang/verus/source/rust_verify_test/tests/`
   and in vstd source. If others use the construct successfully, your problem
   is elsewhere.
4. **Search vstd** — `grep -r` across the entire vstd directory. Check
   `std_specs/` for `assume_specification` on stdlib functions.
5. **Apply an approved workaround** if one matches:
   - `|_|` → `|_e|` (Verus requires named variables in closures)
   - Incompatible derives → `#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]`
   - `debug_assert!` / logging macros → `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` on the statement
6. **Minimal equivalent rewrite** — follow the escalation ladder in Source
   Integrity. Only after isolated repro confirms the specific construct fails.
7. **Stdlib wrapper** — only after isolated repro shows the API call itself
   is the failing unit (see Source Integrity step 4).

### Examples of past false generalizations

| Error on | False conclusion | Reality |
|---|---|---|
| `v.partition_point(\|x\| ...)` | "closures not supported" | `partition_point` lacks vstd spec; closures work fine |
| `v.sort_by_key(\|x\| ...)` | "closures not supported" | `&mut` complex args unsupported; closures work fine |
| `for x in v.windows(2)` | "iterators not supported" | `Windows` lacks `ForLoopGhostIteratorNew`; `for x in vec` works |
| `for i in (0..n).rev()` | "ranges not supported" | `Rev<Range>` lacks trait impl; `for i in 0..n` works |
| `x.ok_or_else(\|\| err)` | "closures not supported" | Works — vstd has `assume_specification` for it |

### Guardrails

**Cfg-gating exec code is cheating.** `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` is only
appropriate for non-semantic items that Verus truly cannot parse:
`derive(Debug)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`).
Do NOT cfg-gate match arms, closures, large code blocks, or expressions.
This makes Verus verify different code than what actually runs.

**Anti-pattern — body duplication (absolutely forbidden):**

```rust
// ❌ WRONG: real body hidden from Verus, replaced with different code
fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> {
    #[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
    { /* real implementation */ }
    #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
    { /* different code that Verus can parse */ }
}
```

**Anti-pattern — function duplication (absolutely forbidden):**

```rust
// ❌ WRONG: entire function gated out, replaced with a different definition
#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* real */ }
#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* different */ }
```

Both patterns verify a **different program** than what ships. The proof is
meaningless. Find a single body that both Rust and Verus accept — or use
`external_body` and document in trust.md.

Partial contracts are always better than none. If 1 out of 5 clauses is
inexpressible, write the other 4.
